title: Rocket Report: SpaceX makes its mark on the Moon; ULA names new boss
gist: This roundup covers rising launch-vehicle failure rates among China, Taiwan, and South Korean startups; growing satellite-industry anxiety that SpaceX may deprioritize commercial Falcon 9 launches after 2028 in favor of Starship/Starlink; a Ukrainian strike on Russia's main rocket factory; new economics research showing the US now launches payload at roughly 1/2 to 1/5 the cost of rivals; and China's Chang'e 7 mission targeting the Moon's south pole.

themes.theme: Launch failures signal growing pains in emerging space programs

insights.claim: China's Long March 7A rocket broke apart less than 90 seconds after liftoff on August 10, but the same YF-100 engines used on that rocket returned to flight successfully just six days later on a Long March 12, and a Long March 5 (also using YF-100 engines) is proceeding with the critical Chang'e 7 lunar mission.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A rapid return-to-flight after a launch failure suggests China's rocket program has redundancy and resilience in its engine supply chain, limiting the disruption from any single vehicle failure to its broader launch cadence.
insights.locator: China’s workhorse Long March rocket family

insights.claim: A prototype satellite launch vehicle from Taiwan's National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST) veered off course shortly after liftoff and triggered its self-destruct mechanism, in the first test flight of Taiwan's military satellite launch program aimed at developing a solid-fueled small-payload rocket.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: An early failure in Taiwan's nascent military launch program is unsurprising for a first test flight, but signals the country remains years from an operational indigenous launch capability, relevant to regional space/defense capability assessments.

insights.claim: South Korean startup Innospace suffered its second consecutive launch failure, with its Sebit suborbital rocket losing control seconds into a test flight from Brazil's Alcântara Space Center and requiring flight termination -- following a similar spin-out failure of its Hanbit-Nano orbital rocket from the same site in December.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Two consecutive failures for Innospace raise doubts about the near-term viability of the company as a credible new launch provider, relevant for assessing competitive risk among smaller international launch startups.
insights.locator: Second failure for South Korea’s Innospace

themes.theme: SpaceX's Falcon 9 retirement risk rattles satellite industry

insights.claim: Commercial satellite operators are increasingly worried SpaceX will retire the Falcon 9 in favor of the still-unproven Starship, and will prioritize its own payloads (Starlink V3 satellites and orbital data centers) over commercial launch customers because of their greater profit potential; the Starship's Starlink-optimized 'Pez' satellite dispenser is cited as evidence of this priority shift.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: If SpaceX deprioritizes third-party commercial launch in favor of its own Starlink/data-center payloads, competing satellite operators would face a serious supply crunch for launch capacity -- a major structural risk to the broader satellite industry's growth plans.

insights.claim: SpaceX's Gwynne Shotwell has previously said Falcon 9's operational lifetime may end in 2030 or 2032, but a source told Ars that SpaceX has informed the US government it intends to end commercial Falcon 9 launches after 2028, continuing to fly it only for a limited number of federally contracted missions thereafter.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A concrete 2028 cutoff for commercial Falcon 9 access -- even if unconfirmed -- gives satellite companies a hard planning deadline; any company relying on Falcon 9 for launches after 2028 faces material execution risk and should be diversifying launch providers now.
insights.locator: SpaceX’s Gwynne Shotwell has previously said

insights.claim: Commercial satellite customers have already begun running into difficulties purchasing Falcon 9 launches scheduled after 2028, making it clear to the industry that they can no longer reliably plan their future around the workhorse rocket.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Real-world booking friction (not just rumor) confirms the Falcon 9 supply risk is already materializing in the market, adding urgency for satellite operators to secure alternative launch capacity or shift timelines.

insights.claim: Ukraine struck Russia's Progress Rocket Space Center in the Samara region using ground-launched Flamingo cruise missiles, hitting a Roscosmos facility involved in electronics production, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A strike roughly 900 km inside Russian territory on the primary manufacturer of the Soyuz-2/Soyuz-5 rockets (used for Russia's crewed spaceflight and military satellites) demonstrates Ukraine's deep-strike capability now threatens core Russian space and defense industrial infrastructure.
insights.quote: In Russia’s Samara region, one of the key enterprises within Roscosmos—the Progress Center, which was involved, among other things, in electronics production–was hit. Flamingo missiles were used. A good achievement.

insights.claim: The Progress Center in Samara builds Russia's Soyuz-2 (about 8 metric tons lift capacity to LEO) and newer Soyuz-5 rockets, plus military satellites; Soyuz-2 is the principal rocket for Russia's human spacecraft launches, raising questions about spillover effects for the International Space Station.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Damage to Russia's sole manufacturer of its crewed-launch rocket creates a direct, quantifiable risk to ISS crew rotation logistics, a scenario NASA and ISS partners would need to monitor closely.

themes.theme: China's reusable rocket progress and US cost dominance

insights.claim: LandSpace's Zhuque-3 rocket successfully landed its first-stage booster downrange in the Gobi Desert on its second flight, making it China's second orbital-class rocket to achieve booster recovery in a little over a month, following a Long March 10B booster recovery in July; several more Chinese companies are expected to attempt booster landings in coming months.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Rapid, multi-company progress toward reusability signals China's launch industry is entering a cost-reduction phase similar to SpaceX's trajectory a decade ago, a leading indicator that Chinese launch costs could fall significantly in coming years.
insights.locator: There’s now a second reusable Chinese rocket

insights.claim: Collectively, Chinese launch companies -- including its largest state-owned enterprises -- only launch about half as often as SpaceX, and do so with an entirely expendable rocket fleet, meaning China's shift toward reusability could substantially close that cadence gap.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Quantifies the current SpaceX cadence advantage (roughly 2x China's combined output) and flags reusability as the key lever that could narrow it -- a metric to track as a proxy for China's growing space-launch competitiveness.

insights.claim: New research published in Economics Letters by UK and Italy-based public policy researchers estimates the average cost to launch a kilogram of payload to orbit is now $3,225 in the United States, versus $5,287 in Japan, $5,809 in China, $6,682 in Russia, $9,897 in Europe, and nearly $15,000 in India.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A concrete, sourced international cost comparison (US at roughly 1/2 Japan's cost, 1/3 Europe's, and 1/5 India's) quantifies SpaceX/Falcon 9 reusability's competitive moat -- critical context for assessing which national launch industries are cost-competitive globally.

insights.claim: Research shows Russia and the United States tracked closely in cumulative payload to orbit by nation for decades, but the US pulled ahead dramatically over the last 10 years amid the Falcon 9 ramp-up in the early 2020s; launch costs in Europe are now three times higher than comparable US payloads, versus roughly similar costs a decade ago.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Documents a historic, data-backed inflection point where Falcon 9's reuse and cadence caused the US to pull decisively ahead of Russia and Europe in launch market share -- a structural, likely durable shift in global space industry competitiveness.

insights.claim: The European Space Agency has quietly killed the Ariane 6 Block 3 upgrade (a lighter carbon-fiber upper stage), after its lightweight Icarus upper stage project failed to win support from ESA member states; a planned Astris orbital transfer 'kick stage' add-on will still become available around 2029 for Ariane 6.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Cancellation of a planned cost/performance upgrade for Europe's flagship rocket, amid already-noted 3x higher launch costs versus the US, suggests Europe's competitive gap versus SpaceX and China is unlikely to close soon.

insights.claim: China's Chang'e 7 mission, launching around August 24 on a Long March 5, will land near Shackleton Crater at the lunar south pole -- one of the most coveted regions of the Moon because its permanently shadowed 'cold traps' are thought to have accumulated water ice and other useful materials over billions of years; the lander is several times larger than NASA-backed probes like Firefly's Blue Ghost.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A larger, more sophisticated Chinese south-pole lunar lander mission targeting the same resource-rich real estate NASA covets for Artemis intensifies the US-China lunar resource competition ahead of any long-term settlement plans.
insights.locator: China will soon launch an ambitious Moon mission

insights.claim: New Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images show a fresh 60-foot-diameter, less-than-10-foot-deep impact crater near Einstein Crater on the Moon, created by a spent Falcon 9 upper stage left in deep space after a 2025 commercial Moon lander launch; asteroid trackers' predicted impact site was accurate to about 0.6 miles.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Confirms asteroid/impact-tracking prediction methods are accurate to sub-mile precision even for small deep-space objects, validating planetary defense tracking capabilities using a real-world test case.
insights.locator: SpaceX’s new scar on the Moon

insights.claim: SpaceX's Starship spacecraft unexpectedly survived splashdown intact in the Indian Ocean after its July 24 test flight, prompting an ad hoc 24-day, several-hundred-mile tow to Australia's Christmas Island, from which SpaceX hopes to eventually return it to Starbase in South Texas.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: An unplanned but intact splashdown recovery gives SpaceX engineers rare hands-on hardware inspection data (especially on the heat shield) that could accelerate progress toward full Starship reusability faster than expected.

themes.theme: ULA leadership change amid Vulcan troubles

insights.claim: United Launch Alliance promoted COO Mark Peller to president and CEO, succeeding Tory Bruno who left in December for Blue Origin; Peller, who joined ULA at its 2006 formation and led Vulcan rocket development, takes over a company whose Vulcan rocket has been grounded since early this year after a second solid rocket booster anomaly in its last three missions.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: New leadership inherits an active vehicle grounding and a recent loss of the Pentagon's preferred-launch-contractor status, making ULA's near-term competitive position -- against SpaceX, Blue Origin, and China -- notably weaker than a year ago.

insights.claim: ULA, a 50-50 Boeing/Lockheed Martin joint venture, lost its long-standing position as the Pentagon's preferred launch contractor last year, and Boeing and Lockheed Martin guaranteed a loan last month to help ULA through 'financial challenges' caused by the Vulcan grounding; it remains unclear if Vulcan will resume launches before year-end.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A parent-company loan guarantee to cover 'financial challenges' is a direct signal of balance-sheet stress at ULA tied to the Vulcan grounding, relevant to assessing Boeing and Lockheed Martin's joint-venture financial exposure.
